subject: science
promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: The rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling
The production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate

questions.lo: The composition of the Earth
questions.q: What is the Earth's core mainly made of?
options: Molten rock called magma
The same rock as the crust
Iron and nickel metal
Water at very high pressure
questions.explain: Yes. The core is mainly iron with some nickel. The outer core is liquid metal and the inner core is solid metal.
optionWhy: You may have thought the core is the magma that comes out of volcanoes. In fact the core is mainly iron and nickel metal; magma is melted rock that forms much nearer the surface.
You may have thought the Earth is made of the same rock all the way through. In fact the Earth is in layers, and the core is mainly iron and nickel, not the rock of the crust.
Yes. The core is mainly iron with some nickel. The outer core is liquid metal and the inner core is solid metal.
You may have thought the deep Earth is full of water. In fact the core is mainly iron and nickel metal; there is no ocean of water inside the Earth.

questions.lo: The composition of the Earth
questions.q: In the Earth's crust, how are most metals found?
options: As lumps or veins of the pure metal
Joined to other elements in compounds
Spread evenly through every kind of rock
As liquid metal that rose from the core
questions.explain: Yes. Most metals are joined to other elements, often oxygen, in compounds. A rock with enough of a metal compound to be worth extracting is called an ore.
optionWhy: You may have thought metals are dug up as shiny metal, like gold nuggets. In fact gold is unusual; most metals, such as iron and aluminium, are found joined to other elements in compounds.
Yes. Most metals are joined to other elements, often oxygen, in compounds. A rock with enough of a metal compound to be worth extracting is called an ore.
You may have thought every rock holds the same metals. In fact metal compounds are concentrated in some rocks, called ores, which is why mines are where they are.
You may have thought the metals in the crust come up from the iron core. In fact the core's metal stays deep inside the Earth; metals in the crust are joined to other elements in compounds.

questions.lo: The composition of the Earth
questions.q: By mass, iron is the most common element in the whole Earth, but oxygen is the most common in the crust. Which explains this?
options: Most of the Earth's iron is in its core
Most of the Earth's iron is in its mantle
Oxygen gas from the air soaks into rocks
Rusting has used up iron in the crust
questions.explain: Yes. Most of the iron is in the core, deep inside the Earth. The crust is made mostly of compounds of oxygen and silicon, so oxygen is its most common element.
optionWhy: Yes. Most of the iron is in the core, deep inside the Earth. The crust is made mostly of compounds of oxygen and silicon, so oxygen is its most common element.
You may have thought the biggest layer must hold most of the iron. In fact the mantle is mostly rock made of compounds of silicon and oxygen; the core is mainly iron and nickel.
You may have thought oxygen is only found as a gas. In fact most of the crust's oxygen is joined to other elements, such as silicon, in the compounds that make up rocks and sand.
You may have thought rusting destroys iron. In fact rust is a compound of iron, so the iron atoms are still there; most of the Earth's iron is in the core.

questions.lo: The structure of the Earth
questions.q: Which statement about the Earth's crust is correct?
options: It is the thickest layer of the Earth
It floats on a layer of liquid magma
It is hotter than the rock below it
It is a thin layer of solid rock
questions.explain: Yes. The crust is solid rock, only about 5–70 km thick. Compared with the whole Earth it is as thin as the skin on an apple.
optionWhy: You may have thought the crust is thick because the ground beneath us seems so deep. In fact it is the thinnest layer; the mantle below it is about 2900 km thick.
You may have thought the crust floats on liquid magma because lava comes out of volcanoes. In fact the mantle below the crust is mostly solid rock that flows very slowly.
You may have thought it gets colder underground because sunlight cannot reach there. In fact rock gets hotter the deeper you go, so the crust is the coolest layer.
Yes. The crust is solid rock, only about 5–70 km thick. Compared with the whole Earth it is as thin as the skin on an apple.

questions.lo: The structure of the Earth
questions.q: The diagram shows the Earth's layers, labelled P, Q, R and S. Which statement about layer R is correct?
options: It is liquid iron and nickel
It is solid iron and nickel
It is liquid rock called magma
It is solid rock, like the crust
questions.explain: Yes. Layer R is the outer core, which is liquid metal, mainly iron and nickel. The inner core, S, is also iron and nickel but is solid.
optionWhy: Yes. Layer R is the outer core, which is liquid metal, mainly iron and nickel. The inner core, S, is also iron and nickel but is solid.
You may have thought the whole core is one solid ball of metal. In fact the outer core, R, is liquid metal; only the inner core, S, is solid.
You may have thought the liquid inside the Earth is magma. In fact the outer core is liquid metal, mainly iron and nickel; magma is melted rock, which forms much nearer the surface.
You may have thought the inside of the Earth is solid rock all the way through, like the crust. In fact the Earth has layers: layer R, the outer core, is liquid metal, mainly iron and nickel.

questions.lo: The structure of the Earth
questions.q: Lava pours out of a volcano. A pupil says this shows that the whole mantle is liquid. Which statement is correct?
options: The mantle is a sea of liquid magma
The lava rises up from the Earth's core
Most of the mantle is solid rock
Rock gets colder the deeper you go
questions.explain: Yes. The mantle is very hot but mostly solid rock, which can flow very slowly over millions of years. Magma forms only where a small amount of rock melts, near the top of the mantle or in the crust.
optionWhy: You may have thought lava shows there is a liquid layer under the crust. In fact the mantle is mostly solid; lava comes from small amounts of melted rock near the top of the mantle or in the crust.
You may have thought volcanoes are fed from the core. In fact the core is metal, far below; the molten rock in volcanoes forms much nearer the surface.
Yes. The mantle is very hot but mostly solid rock, which can flow very slowly over millions of years. Magma forms only where a small amount of rock melts, near the top of the mantle or in the crust.
You may have thought the inside of the Earth is cold because the Sun cannot heat it. In fact rock gets hotter with depth, which is why some rock near the top of the mantle can melt.

questions.lo: The rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
questions.q: How does sedimentary rock form?
options: Wet mud and sand just dry out and harden
Layers of sediment are squashed and cemented
Sediment melts near a volcano, then cools again
It rises up from deep inside the Earth
questions.explain: Yes. Sediment settles in layers, and the weight of new layers squashes (compacts) it. Minerals from the water then cement the grains together.
optionWhy: You may have thought mud and sand turn to rock just by drying, like mud in the sun. In fact the sediment must be squashed by the layers above it and cemented together, over a very long time.
Yes. Sediment settles in layers, and the weight of new layers squashes (compacts) it. Minerals from the water then cement the grains together.
You may have thought all rock needs the heat of a volcano. In fact sedimentary rock forms without melting; rock that melts and then cools becomes igneous rock.
You may have thought rocks come up from deep inside the Earth. In fact sedimentary rock is made from sediment laid down in layers on the surface, which is then buried.

questions.lo: The rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
questions.q: The diagram shows water in a crack in a rock. The water freezes and thaws many times. What is this an example of?
options: Chemical weathering
Physical weathering
Erosion of the rock
Metamorphism by ice
questions.explain: Yes. Water expands when it freezes, so the ice pushes the crack wider; after many freezes, pieces break off. The rock is broken up and no new substance forms.
optionWhy: You may have thought any weathering involving water is chemical. In fact here the water only freezes and melts; no new substance forms, so this is physical weathering.
Yes. Water expands when it freezes, so the ice pushes the crack wider; after many freezes, pieces break off. The rock is broken up and no new substance forms.
You may have thought breaking rock up is erosion. In fact breaking rock where it is, is weathering; erosion is when the broken pieces are carried away, for example by rivers or wind.
You may have thought any change to a rock is metamorphism. In fact metamorphism happens deep underground, by heat and pressure; ice splitting rock at the surface is weathering.

questions.lo: The rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
questions.q: The diagram shows layers of rock near the top of a mountain. One layer contains fossil sea shells. What does this suggest?
options: People carried the shells up the mountain
The shells were pushed up from the core
The layer formed from sediment on a sea bed
The layer formed when volcanic lava cooled
questions.explain: Yes. The shells were buried in sediment on a sea bed, which became sedimentary rock. Over millions of years the rock was pushed up to form part of a mountain.
optionWhy: You may have thought people must have moved the shells there. In fact the shells are inside the rock layer, so they were buried as the rock formed; the rock was later pushed up.
You may have thought rocks and fossils come up from deep inside the Earth. In fact the core is metal, far below; these shells were buried in sediment on a sea bed.
Yes. The shells were buried in sediment on a sea bed, which became sedimentary rock. Over millions of years the rock was pushed up to form part of a mountain.
You may have thought rock layers form from lava. In fact hot lava would destroy shells; almost all fossils are found in sedimentary rock, made from sediment laid down in layers.

questions.lo: The rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
questions.q: The diagram shows close-up drawings of granite and basalt. Which statement is correct?
options: Granite's magma cooled more slowly
Basalt's magma cooled more slowly
Both are cemented grains of sediment
Both magmas cooled at the same rate
questions.explain: Yes. Granite has large crystals, so its magma cooled slowly, deep underground, giving the crystals time to grow. Basalt has small crystals because its lava cooled quickly at the surface.
optionWhy: Yes. Granite has large crystals, so its magma cooled slowly, deep underground, giving the crystals time to grow. Basalt has small crystals because its lava cooled quickly at the surface.
You may have thought quick cooling makes bigger crystals. In fact slow cooling gives crystals more time to grow, so granite, with the larger crystals, cooled more slowly.
You may have thought rocks full of crystals are grains stuck together, like sandstone. In fact these crystals grew and locked together as molten rock cooled, so both rocks are igneous.
You may have thought crystal size has nothing to do with cooling. In fact the different crystal sizes show the two cooled at different rates; slower cooling gives larger crystals.

The right square, labelled basalt, is filled by about 150 tiny crystals that fit tightly together. A note below says both drawn at the same scale.

questions.lo: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling
questions.q: Coal and metal ores are called limited, or finite, resources. Why?
options: Only a few countries may mine them
They form far too slowly to be replaced
There is only a small amount of each
Using them destroys the atoms in them
questions.explain: Yes. Coal and ores formed over millions of years, far too slowly to be replaced. So there is a fixed amount, and once it has been used it will run out.
optionWhy: You may have thought 'limited' means only some countries are allowed them, as in 'limited access'. In fact a limited (finite) resource has a fixed amount in the Earth that will one day run out.
Yes. Coal and ores formed over millions of years, far too slowly to be replaced. So there is a fixed amount, and once it has been used it will run out.
You may have thought finite means there is only a little. In fact there may be a lot left; finite means the amount is fixed and is not being replaced.
You may have thought using a material destroys its atoms. In fact atoms are never destroyed: burning coal turns its carbon into carbon dioxide. Coal and ores are finite because they are not replaced.

questions.lo: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling
questions.q: Example figures for 1 kg of a metal: making it from ore uses 170 MJ (megajoules). Recycling scrap uses 4 MJ to collect it and 10 MJ to melt it. How much energy does recycling save?
options: 156 MJ
160 MJ
166 MJ
170 MJ
questions.explain: Yes. Recycling uses 4 MJ + 10 MJ = 14 MJ. That is 170 MJ − 14 MJ = 156 MJ less than making the metal from ore.
optionWhy: Yes. Recycling uses 4 MJ + 10 MJ = 14 MJ. That is 170 MJ − 14 MJ = 156 MJ less than making the metal from ore.
You may have counted only the energy for melting the scrap. In fact collecting it also uses energy, so the saving is 170 MJ − 10 MJ − 4 MJ = 156 MJ.
You may have thought recycled metal is simply reused as it is. In fact the scrap must be melted, which uses 10 MJ as well as the 4 MJ to collect it.
You may have thought recycling uses no energy at all. In fact collecting and melting the scrap use 14 MJ, so the saving is 156 MJ, not the whole 170 MJ.

questions.lo: Earth as a source of limited resources and the efficacy of recycling
questions.q: Which of these is a renewable resource?
options: Wood, because new trees can be planted
Aluminium, because cans can be recycled
Coal, because plants keep on growing
Iron ore, because there is so much of it
questions.explain: Yes. A renewable resource can be replaced as fast as we use it. New trees can be grown to replace those cut down.
optionWhy: Yes. A renewable resource can be replaced as fast as we use it. New trees can be grown to replace those cut down.
You may have thought anything that can be recycled is renewable. In fact aluminium comes from ore, which is finite; recycling makes it last longer but does not make new aluminium.
You may have thought coal keeps forming because plants keep growing. In fact coal formed from plants buried over millions of years, far too slowly to replace what we burn.
You may have thought a resource is renewable if there is a lot of it. In fact iron ore formed over millions of years and is not being replaced; there is a lot, but it is finite.

questions.lo: The composition of the atmosphere
questions.q: About what percentage of dry air is carbon dioxide?
options: About 0.04%
About 0.9%
About 4%
About 21%
questions.explain: Yes. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of dry air, roughly 4 particles in every 10 000. Even so, it has an important effect on the Earth's temperature.
optionWhy: Yes. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of dry air, roughly 4 particles in every 10 000. Even so, it has an important effect on the Earth's temperature.
You may have thought carbon dioxide is the third most common gas in air. In fact that is argon, at about 0.9%; carbon dioxide is only about 0.04%.
You may have remembered that the air we breathe out has about 4% carbon dioxide. In fact the air around us has only about 0.04%, a hundred times less.
You may have thought carbon dioxide is a large part of the air because it is talked about so much. In fact about 21% is oxygen; carbon dioxide is only about 0.04%.

questions.lo: The composition of the atmosphere
questions.q: Dry air contains nitrogen (N₂), oxygen (O₂), argon (Ar) and carbon dioxide (CO₂). Which describes dry air?
options: A mixture of elements and a compound
A mixture of compounds and an element
Nitrogen and oxygen joined together
A pure substance when it is clean
questions.explain: Yes. N₂, O₂ and Ar each contain one type of atom, so they are elements; CO₂ is a compound. They are not joined to each other, so air is a mixture.
optionWhy: Yes. N₂, O₂ and Ar each contain one type of atom, so they are elements; CO₂ is a compound. They are not joined to each other, so air is a mixture.
You may have thought N₂ and O₂ are compounds because their molecules have two atoms. In fact each has only one type of atom, so they are elements; only CO₂ here is a compound.
You may have thought gases together make a compound. In fact the nitrogen and oxygen molecules in air are not joined to each other, so air is a mixture.
You may have thought clean air is 'pure'. In everyday language it is, but in science a pure substance has only one substance in it; air has several, so it is a mixture.

questions.lo: The composition of the atmosphere
questions.q: Which statement about dry air is correct?
options: Oxygen makes up about four-fifths of it
Nitrogen makes up about four-fifths of it
Carbon dioxide makes up about a fifth of it
Its nitrogen and oxygen are chemically joined
questions.explain: Yes. Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, roughly four-fifths. Oxygen is about 21%, roughly one-fifth.
optionWhy: You may have thought air is mostly oxygen because we breathe it in. In fact oxygen is only about a fifth of air; about four-fifths is nitrogen.
Yes. Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, roughly four-fifths. Oxygen is about 21%, roughly one-fifth.
You may have thought carbon dioxide is a large part of air. In fact it is only about 0.04%; about a fifth of the air is oxygen.
You may have thought air is a compound of nitrogen and oxygen. In fact the nitrogen and oxygen molecules in air are separate, so air is a mixture.

questions.lo: The production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
questions.q: The graph shows carbon dioxide in the air, measured in Hawaii from 1960 to 2020. What is the main cause of this rise?
options: More and more people breathing out
The hole in the ozone layer
Rubbish and litter in streets
Burning coal, oil and natural gas
questions.explain: Yes. Coal, oil and gas are fossil fuels. Burning them releases carbon that was stored underground for millions of years, and this is the main cause of the rise.
optionWhy: You may have thought breathing out adds the extra carbon dioxide. In fact the carbon we breathe out comes from food made by plants that recently took carbon dioxide from the air, so it adds none overall.
You may have thought the ozone hole is linked to carbon dioxide. In fact the ozone hole was caused by other gases (CFCs) and does not add carbon dioxide to the air.
You may have thought any pollution, such as litter, adds to global warming. In fact litter is not the cause of this rise in carbon dioxide; burning fossil fuels is.
Yes. Coal, oil and gas are fossil fuels. Burning them releases carbon that was stored underground for millions of years, and this is the main cause of the rise.

questions.lo: The production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
questions.q: Large areas of rainforest are cut down and burned. Why does this add to global warming?
options: Less oxygen in the air makes the Earth warmer
It makes the hole in the ozone layer bigger
Burning the wood adds carbon dioxide to the air
The heat from the fires warms up the whole planet
questions.explain: Yes. Burning the wood releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. With fewer trees, less carbon dioxide is also taken in by photosynthesis.
optionWhy: You may have thought forests matter for climate because they make oxygen. In fact oxygen is not a greenhouse gas, and losing it would not warm the Earth; burning forests adds carbon dioxide, which is a greenhouse gas.
You may have thought cutting forests damages the ozone layer. In fact the ozone hole was caused by other gases (CFCs); forest loss warms the Earth by adding carbon dioxide.

questions.lo: The production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate
questions.q: Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of the air. Can a rise in this small amount change the climate, and why?
options: No, as 0.04% is far too little to matter
Yes, as CO₂ absorbs heat from the Earth
Yes, as it is a poison that pollutes the air
No, as CO₂ does not absorb any heat at all
questions.explain: Yes. Carbon dioxide absorbs heat given off by the Earth, so even a small rise traps more heat. It has risen from about 0.028% before 1800 to about 0.042% in 2024, and the Earth has warmed.
optionWhy: You may have thought such a small amount cannot matter. In fact carbon dioxide absorbs heat strongly, so a small rise in it is enough to warm the Earth.
Yes. Carbon dioxide absorbs heat given off by the Earth, so even a small rise traps more heat. It has risen from about 0.028% before 1800 to about 0.042% in 2024, and the Earth has warmed.
You may have thought carbon dioxide warms the Earth because it is a poison. In fact at this level it is harmless to breathe; it warms the Earth because it absorbs heat.

questions.q: As the Earth's average temperature rises, which change do scientists expect?
options: Sea level rises as ice melts
Sea level falls as seas evaporate
Earthquakes become more common
Rivers fill up with more litter
questions.explain: Yes. Ice on land melts and seawater expands as it warms, so sea level rises. It has already risen by about 20 cm since 1900.
optionWhy: Yes. Ice on land melts and seawater expands as it warms, so sea level rises. It has already risen by about 20 cm since 1900.
You may have thought warmer seas would dry up. In fact the extra water from melting land ice, and the expansion of warmer seawater, make sea level rise.
You may have thought global warming causes earthquakes. In fact earthquakes are caused mainly by movements of the Earth's tectonic plates; they are not an expected result of a warmer climate.
You may have thought global warming and litter are the same kind of pollution. In fact warming does not make litter; expected changes include rising sea level and more heatwaves.
